awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: The Effect of Contact on Culture Change
awd_abstract_narration:
This doctoral dissertation project investigates processes of cultural change in the past that take place when multiple complex societies coalesce and re-shape social and economic ways of life. Given present day situations as a consequence of population movement as a result of war and violence, archaeology can help to understand how such populations negotiate aspects of their lives through material culture over multiple centuries. Archaeological ceramic analysis is well suited to study this phenomenon because it can yield information on how communities’ choices in production, consumption, and use changed or stayed the same before and after cultural contact events. These choices often reflect social and economic affiliations of group members. Data from this project offers insights into how human populations adapt to social change, providing valuable perspectives for contemporary issues of migration and cultural integration. This study contributes to a growing body of evidence showing societies have a wide range of responses to both external stimuli and internal negotiations. The project produces new knowledge on adaptations to growing issues of culture contact experienced today and provides information to partners on ancestral practices and land use. The researchers are working with community organizations to integrate analytical perspectives, give local presentations and museum exhibits, and improve public understanding of archaeological science and the scientific method.  

The research examines how choices in ceramic production, consumption, and use were mediated when inhabitants interacted with a very early city site. The project examines the specific ways in which societies created pottery before and after this period of flux. Potting choices are examined using macroscopic, microscopic, and geochemical analyses. This project integrates chemical data collected via neutron activation analysis (NAA) and laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) as well as mineralogical data collected from ceramic petrography. These analyses create a detailed picture of natural resource utilization through time and highlight how social learning and technological choices were negotiated.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Throughout our lives, our ideas, personalities, and practices are shaped by our interactions with people, places, and things. Cultural movements, new technologies, and migration are examples of experiences where our ideas may clash with others, leading to changes in how we view ourselves and the world around us.
Archaeologically, we can see the results of these episodes of contact through the objects created and consumed through these relationships. These objects are more than things people made and used; they provide evidence for how people responded to new ideas, technologies, and traditions. By examining how objects were made, used, and changed over time, archaeologists can better understand how people navigated periods of cultural change. This research examined these processes through pottery made by Indigenous communities in the Central Mississippi River Valley (CMRV) around 1,000 years ago.Around AD 1050, Cahokia emerged near present-day St. Louis, Missouri. Indigenous groups from throughout what is now the United States migrated to and lived together in this large city, participating in a large-scale religious movement. Cahokia’s massive earthen mounds, aligned with the movements of the sun and moon, helped bring religious realms associated with gods and ancestors into the world of people. Physical manifestations of this movement included pottery made with crushed shell temper, houses constructed using pre-made walls placed into long trenches, and a suite of religious symbols.
This research suggests that some people from the CMRV may have moved to Cahokia to participate in this broader cultural movement. Pottery vessels known as Varney Red, commonly found in the CMRV, are also found in small numbers throughout Greater Cahokia, including at the East St. Louis and Halliday sites. Although these vessels were made using local clays, they were produced using techniques similar to those identified at Zebree in the CMRV. At Halliday, on the outskirts of Greater Cahokia, people appear to have followed the forms and decorations used in the CMRV more closely. At East St. Louis, closer to Cahokia’s administrative center, potters were more flexible. They maintained the general form of CMRV vessels but added features common at Cahokia, such as protruding lips and red slip on the outside of the vessel. These differences suggest that people who moved to Cahokia participated in local traditions while adapting their pottery to their new surroundings.
Cultural change also affected those who remained in their home communities, who likely encountered new ideas through their connections with people who traveled to Cahokia. At Hoecake, this research shows that around the time of Cahokia’s rise, inhabitants established a village where they began incorporating shell temper into their pottery. Rather than abandoning their existing traditions, they combined shell with grog, a material they had used in pottery production for hundreds of years. The site also shows that some households adopted new Mississippian pottery practices more readily than others.
At Zebree, new radiocarbon dates suggest that part of the village was abandoned shortly before and during the rise of Cahokia. Approximately 100 years later, the village grew substantially and included structures, pottery, and stone tools that were similar to those found at Cahokia. Before this gap in occupation, Zebree’s inhabitants primarily made cordmarked pottery. After the village was reoccupied, approximately half of the pottery consisted of locally made Varney Red painted jars and pans. Rather than simply copying red-slipped pottery from Cahokia, these vessels combined local traditions with new practices. They retained forms common in the CMRV while incorporating red slip and shell temper associated with Cahokian pottery. By combining white shell and red slip, materials that could carry important symbolic and religious meanings within Indigenous communities, Zebree’s potters created vessels that connected different religious realms while expressing their own local identities.
In summary, the cases from Zebree and Hoecake show that pottery provided a means for people to participate in the broader Mississippian world while maintaining connections to their homeland. These findings demonstrate that cultural change was not simply a process of adopting new traditions. Instead, communities actively adapted, combined, and reinterpreted new ideas through their existing practices.
The themes and results of this dissertation can help us understand how populations negotiate different aspects of their lives during times of war and violence, with the goal of improving social cohesion and quality of life, especially for migrant communities. In addition to the submitted dissertation, the results are being prepared as a book manuscript and presented at academic conferences. They have also been presented to Indigenous Nations whose ancestral lands include these archaeological sites, engaging them with research about their ancestors and heritage. Clays from their homeland were given to tribes for activities that look to continue or revive ancestral pottery practices. Additionally, lectures given by the co-PI to communities near these sites and the University of Florida have helped spread awareness of archaeological science and its applications.
